sections.section_title: Initial presentation after dog bite: sepsis, DIC, and early management
sections.description: Covers the patient’s timeline from canine exposure to ICU care, introduces Capnocytophaga canimorsus as the pathogen, and explains the early focus on sepsis/DIC-directed therapy and multiorgan support.
subtopics: Exposure and incubation: dog bite to upper lip; missed outpatient penicillin; rapid evolution to fever >40 °C, malaise, mottled/cool extremities, refractory hypoglycaemia
Admission findings: qSOFA context; lactic acidosis and metabolic acidaemia; pancytopenia; coagulopathy; acute kidney injury; elevated liver enzymes; urinalysis with protein and blood

Capnocytophaga canimorsus essentials: dog/cat oropharyngeal reservoir; encapsulated, slow-growing gram-negative rod; variable presentations from meningitis to fulminant sepsis/DIC; delayed culture positivity and role of molecular methods; mortality risk

Initial differential and consultations: DIC secondary to bacteraemia prioritized; surgical causes (eg, necrotising fasciitis) excluded clinically/radiologically; haematology considered acute leukaemia/HLH/HUS; flow cytometry normal and bone marrow biopsy cancelled

ICU course and organ support: progression to anuria despite fluids/diuretics; septic cardiomyopathy with fluid overload; initiation of CRRT; transfusion support (platelets/fibrinogen); stress-dose corticosteroids; albumin; distal acral ischaemia and ecchymoses consistent with microthrombi in DIC

Antimicrobial strategy: empiric piperacillin/tazobactam to cover dog-associated flora (including Capnocytophaga); subsequent culture confirmation of C. canimorsus; de-escalation to ampicillin then oral penicillin

sections.section_title: From resolving sepsis to thrombotic microangiopathy: recognizing and diagnosing CM-HUS
sections.description: Explains the clinical turning point when isolated haemolysis emerged, how clinicians distinguished TMA from DIC, and the stepwise diagnostic workup culminating in a diagnosis of complement-mediated HUS.
subtopics: Clinical inflection point: new isolated haemoglobin fall (111 → 68 g/L) with persistently low platelets, rising LDH, undetectable haptoglobin, no overt bleeding, and stabilising inflammatory/coagulation profile

Pitfalls with DAT: initial IgG-positive DAT raising autoimmune haemolysis concern; lack of steroid response; recognition of false positivity from penicillin or recent transfusions; repeat DAT negative
Peripheral smear evidence: 15%–20% schistocytes confirming MAHA and prompting TMA evaluation
Distinguishing TMA from DIC: improving coagulation tests with ongoing MAHA/thrombocytopenia favors TMA; clinical context and timing after initial sepsis improvement

Adult TMA algorithm: urgent exclusion of TTP (PLASMIC score use; ADAMTS13 activity 43.5% excludes TTP); initiate plasma exchange as a bridge while awaiting key labs; stool PCR negative for Shiga toxin excludes STEC-HUS
Complement testing nuances: normal C3/C4 and normal pathway screens early do not exclude CM-HUS; timing relative to PEX/eculizumab affects interpretation

Kidney biopsy to confirm TMA: performed after platelets improved (77×10^9/L); findings of ischaemic glomeruli with fibrin thrombi, severe acute tubular necrosis, scattered crescents; no immune complex deposition on IF; EM without primary glomerulopathy
Diagnostic synthesis: exclusion of TTP/STEC-HUS, biopsy-proven TMA, and subsequent response to eculizumab supporting complement-mediated HUS triggered by infection

sections.section_title: Pathophysiology of complement-mediated HUS and infectious triggers
sections.description: Builds the mechanistic framework for CM-HUS with emphasis on alternative complement pathway dysregulation, genetic susceptibility, and how Capnocytophaga infection can precipitate endothelial injury and TMA.
subtopics: Alternative pathway overview: continuous low-grade C3 activation; regulation by factor H, factor I, membrane cofactor protein (CD46), and factor B; terminal pathway culminating in C5b-9
Endothelial injury and TMA: uncontrolled complement activation on microvascular endothelium leads to platelet activation, fibrin-rich microthrombi, MAHA, and kidney-predominant injury
Genetic predisposition and penetrance: variants/autoantibodies in CFH, CFI, CFB, C3, CD46 present in 50%–70% but require a trigger; incomplete penetrance
Infectious ‘second hits’: common triggers (respiratory/enteric infections, pregnancy, autoimmune disease, drugs) and rare triggers like Capnocytophaga

Capnocytophaga–complement interface: capsule-mediated variability in serum susceptibility; complement as key host defense; paradox wherein robust complement activation clears bacteria but can precipitate CM-HUS in susceptible hosts

Applying to this case: extended testing with markedly reduced AH50 after PEX/eculizumab reflects treatment effect rather than baseline deficiency; normal C3/C4 during disease does not exclude CM-HUS; negative anti–factor H antibodies; no pathogenic complement variants identified
Literature context: prior reports (eg, factor B variant case) versus this infection-triggered, gene-negative presentation; implications for prognosis and duration of therapy

sections.section_title: Therapeutic strategy in CM-HUS with recent bacteraemia: timing, bridging, and infection risk mitigation
sections.description: Details the stepwise management: antimicrobial therapy for Capnocytophaga, when and how to use plasma exchange and eculizumab, vaccination/antibiotic prophylaxis around complement blockade, and organ-supportive care.
subtopics: Definitive antimicrobials for Capnocytophaga: empiric broad coverage with piperacillin/tazobactam, then targeted ampicillin/penicillin; principles of de-escalation once cultures identify pathogen

Plasma exchange as a bridge: immediate initiation when TTP cannot be excluded; transient benefit in CM-HUS by removing inflammatory/complement factors; stopping once TTP excluded and complement blockade initiated
Eculizumab for CM-HUS: indications, early initiation to improve renal outcomes; induction (900 mg IV weekly ×4) and maintenance (1200 mg IV q2 weeks) used in this case

Vaccination and prophylaxis: MenACWY (Menveo) and MenB (Bexsero) prior to blockade when feasible; antibiotic prophylaxis (eg, penicillin) if starting within 2 weeks of vaccination; counselling on infection risk

Timing relative to bacteraemia: initiating complement blockade after negative blood cultures to balance control of TMA with risk of uncontrolled infection by encapsulated organisms (Neisseria, Capnocytophaga)
Supportive care: CRRT for anuric AKI and fluid overload; RBC transfusions for anaemia; platelet/fibrinogen support in DIC; steroid trial discontinued once immune haemolysis was excluded

Monitoring response and safety: platelets, LDH, haptoglobin, schistocytes, creatinine, urine output; vigilance for invasive infections during C5 blockade; documentation of complement testing timing relative to PEX/eculizumab
Duration and discontinuation planning: factoring severity at presentation, renal recovery, and genetic results; structured reassessment for taper/cessation with relapse monitoring

sections.description: Summarizes the patient’s recovery trajectory, discusses prognostic determinants in CM-HUS, and distills practical takeaways and an approach clinicians can generalize to similar cases.
subtopics: Patient outcome: return of diuresis after PEX; sustained haematologic remission and partial renal recovery after eculizumab; creatinine ~175 µmol/L; dialysis independence; ongoing maintenance eculizumab with outpatient follow-up
Prognostic factors: time-to-eculizumab initiation, baseline renal injury (dialysis dependence), histologic severity, and presence/absence of pathogenic complement variants

Key clinical pearls: consider CM-HUS when MAHA emerges as sepsis/DIC improve; normal C3/C4 do not exclude CM-HUS; beware false-positive DAT from penicillins/transfusions; use PEX while excluding TTP; initiate complement blockade promptly once CM-HUS is likely

Infection risk management under complement blockade: vaccinate, provide antibiotic prophylaxis if vaccines are recent, avoid starting during active bacteraemia when possible, and educate patients on urgent evaluation for fever

Zoonosis-specific lesson: following dog bites, include Capnocytophaga in the differential for rapidly progressive sepsis with DIC and potential TMA; early, appropriate empiric antibiotics are critical

Systems/diagnostic considerations: anticipate culture delays with fastidious organisms; use molecular diagnostics when available; maintain a clear TMA workup pathway that integrates clinical scores, targeted labs, and biopsy when safe
